source.section: Number of Factors and Sum of all Factors

problem.text: Compute the sum of all positive integers whose positive divisors sum to $186$.

steps.title: Where to start: the divisor sum splits into factors
steps.body:
If $n = p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2}\cdots$, the sum of its divisors is a product with one factor for each prime:
$$\sigma(n) = (1 + p_1 + \cdots + p_1^{e_1})(1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_2^{e_2})\cdots$$
We are told this product is $186$. So we should factor $186$ and ask which pieces can be the sum of powers of one prime.

steps.title: Which factors are allowed?
steps.body: Each factor $1 + p + \cdots + p^{e}$ is at least $1 + 2 = 3$, so no factor can be $2$. That means the $2$ in $186$ must be glued to another prime. The possible ways to split $186$ are then $186$ itself, $6\cdot 31$, and $3\cdot 62$.

your_turn.prompt: Can $186$ itself be $1 + p + \cdots + p^e$ for a single prime $p$? Try $e = 1$ and $e = 2$.
your_turn.answer: No. $e = 1$ needs $p = 185$, which is not prime, and $p^2 + p + 1 = 186$ has no integer solution ($13^2 + 13 + 1 = 183$). Larger $e$ also misses.

steps.title: The split $6\cdot 31$
steps.body: The only way to get $6$ is $1 + 5$, so one prime is $5$ with exponent $1$. For $31$ there are two options: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16$ and $1 + 5 + 25$. Careful: the second one uses the prime $5$ again, which is already taken, so only the powers of $2$ work.

your_turn.prompt: Which number $n$ does this case give?

steps.title: The split $3\cdot 62$
steps.body: The only way to get $3$ is $1 + 2$, so one prime is $2$ with exponent $1$. For $62$, the option $1 + 61$ works because $61$ is prime, while $p^2 + p + 1 = 62$ has no integer solution.

your_turn.prompt: Which number $n$ does this case give?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Exactly two numbers have divisor sum $186$: $80$ and $122$. Their sum is $80 + 122 = 202$. The answer is **202**.
